domain.title: Security
domain.summary: Protecting systems and data by understanding where trust changes hands and how attackers exploit misplaced assumptions.

concepts.title: Trust boundaries
concepts.summary: A trust boundary is anywhere data or control crosses from a less trusted party to a more trusted one; every crossing needs checks.
learningObjectives: Identify the trust boundaries a request crosses in a given change
Explain why anything from a client, webhook, or third party is untrusted
Locate where validation and authorization belong relative to each boundary
recognitionSignals: fields the server should derive itself, such as userId, role, price, or tenantId, read from the request body or form
webhook or callback handlers, and whether they verify a signature before acting
handlers that trust hidden form fields, client-computed totals, or flags set by the frontend
responses from third-party APIs, internal services, or LLMs used without checks in privileged operations
misconceptionPatterns: Treating data from your own frontend as trusted
Assuming internal services never send malicious input
Believing TypeScript types act as a trust boundary
Trusting a webhook payload because it arrived at an unguessable URL, without verifying its signature

concepts.title: Input validation
concepts.summary: Checking that untrusted input has the expected shape, type, and bounds before code relies on it.
learningObjectives: Validate untrusted payloads with a schema at the boundary
Distinguish allow-listing from deny-listing
Identify missing bounds such as length, range, and array size
recognitionSignals: schema validation at a request, form, or message boundary (e.g. Zod, Valibot, JSON Schema, Pydantic)
deserialized request payloads or form data used without schema parsing, including type assertions such as `as T`
request bodies spread or passed whole into ORM create or update calls
file uploads or user-supplied sizes, counts, or page limits
misconceptionPatterns: Validating only on the client
Casting parsed JSON to a type instead of validating it
Validating format but not size or quantity
Believing per-field format checks are enough when the whole request body is passed to a create or update

concepts.title: Injection
concepts.summary: When untrusted data is spliced into text that an interpreter parses — SQL, shell commands, HTML/JavaScript, or file paths — it can change the structure of what runs; the defense is APIs that keep data separate from code, such as bound parameters, argument arrays, and context-aware output encoding.

related.boundary: Instructions injected into an LLM's context map there; there is no parameterization equivalent.

learningObjectives: Explain why a parameterized query prevents SQL injection while string concatenation or interpolation does not
Identify the injection sink (SQL, shell command, HTML, file path) and the untrusted source that feeds it in a change
Predict how an attacker-controlled value changes the resulting query, command, markup, or path
Choose the safe API for a given sink, such as bound parameters, execFile with an argument array, or context-aware output encoding, and defend the choice over sanitizing input
recognitionSignals: SQL built by string concatenation or template interpolation, or unsafe raw-query helpers (e.g. $queryRawUnsafe, knex.raw, cursor.execute with f-strings)
ORDER BY, column, or table names taken from request input
shell execution with interpolated arguments (exec/execSync, subprocess with shell=True, os.system)
raw HTML sinks fed user content (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML, v-html, |safe or unescaped template tags)
file-system paths built from user input without normalizing and checking the resolved path
misconceptionPatterns: Believing input validation alone prevents injection
Believing that because an app uses an ORM, strings interpolated into its raw-query helpers are safe
Believing query placeholders can safely parameterize identifiers such as column names, table names, or sort direction
Believing framework auto-escaping also protects raw-HTML APIs and user-supplied URLs placed in href or src attributes

concepts.title: Secrets management
concepts.summary: Keeping credentials such as API keys and private keys out of source, logs, and clients, and able to be rotated.
learningObjectives: Identify secrets that could leak through source control, logs, error messages, or client bundles
Explain how environment-based configuration keeps secrets out of code
Describe what rotation requires and why long-lived static credentials are risky
recognitionSignals: secret values placed in client-exposed environment prefixes (NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_, PUBLIC_) or imported into client-side code
hard-coded strings resembling API keys, private keys, or connection strings with passwords
.env files, credential files, or keys added to the repository, build arguments, or container images
credentials included in error messages, API responses, or logged headers and configuration
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a private repository makes committed secrets safe
Assuming environment variables are never exposed to the browser
Deleting a leaked secret from git without rotating it

concepts.title: Password and token handling
concepts.summary: Storing passwords with slow hashes, issuing and verifying tokens correctly, and limiting what a stolen credential can do.
learningObjectives: Explain why passwords are hashed with slow, salted algorithms rather than encrypted
Evaluate token lifetime, storage location, and revocation for a session design
Identify token verification mistakes such as skipping signature, expiry, or audience checks, or accepting the algorithm named in the token
Identify reset tokens, session IDs, or API keys generated with a non-cryptographic random source
recognitionSignals: password hashing or comparison (bcrypt, scrypt, argon2, PBKDF2), or passwords passed to fast hashes such as MD5, SHA-1, or SHA-256
JWT or session-token sign, verify, and decode calls, including algorithm, expiry, and audience options
session cookies set with or without httpOnly and secure, or tokens stored in localStorage
tokens, reset codes, or keys generated with Math.random or other non-cryptographic randomness
misconceptionPatterns: Believing reversible encoding or encryption is an acceptable way to store passwords
Believing a fast hash such as SHA-256 is adequate for password storage as long as it is salted
Trusting a JWT's claims after decoding it without verifying the signature with a pinned algorithm, expiry, and audience
Assuming long-lived tokens are harmless if transmitted over HTTPS

concepts.title: Least privilege
concepts.summary: Each user, service, and token should have only the access it needs, so any single compromise has a limited blast radius.
learningObjectives: Identify over-broad permissions requested by a token, role, or integration
Explain blast radius using a concrete compromised-credential scenario
Design a narrower permission set for a service or integration
recognitionSignals: OAuth scopes or GitHub App permission lists
database users or IAM roles
admin or service-role clients used in request handlers
shared credentials across environments
misconceptionPatterns: Requesting broad scopes 'in case we need them later'
Using a superuser database connection for application traffic
Assuming internal tools do not need access control

concepts.title: Request forgery (CSRF and SSRF)
concepts.summary: Confused-deputy attacks that borrow someone else's authority: CSRF makes a victim's browser send a state-changing request carrying its cookies, and SSRF makes your server send a request from inside your network to a destination the attacker chooses.
learningObjectives: Explain why a cookie-authenticated, state-changing endpoint is exposed to CSRF and how SameSite, Origin checks, and anti-CSRF tokens each reduce that exposure
Distinguish what CORS controls (which origins may read responses) from what CSRF defenses control (whether a cross-site request is honored)
Identify server-side fetches of user-influenced URLs as SSRF risks and predict what an attacker could reach, such as internal services or cloud metadata endpoints
Compare SSRF defenses such as destination allow-lists, blocking private address ranges after DNS resolution, and disabling redirects
recognitionSignals: state-changing handlers (POST/PUT/DELETE, server actions, or state-changing GETs) authenticated only by cookies
SameSite cookie attributes, anti-CSRF tokens, or Origin/Referer checks
server code fetching, proxying, or previewing URLs taken from request input or stored user data (image proxies, link unfurlers, user-configured webhook URLs)
misconceptionPatterns: Believing CORS stops a cross-site request from being sent and acted on, rather than only controlling whether the response can be read
Believing SameSite=Lax makes every cookie-authenticated endpoint immune to CSRF
Believing a string check on a URL's hostname is enough to prevent SSRF despite redirects, DNS rebinding, and alternate IP encodings

concepts.title: Third-party dependency risk
concepts.summary: Every package, action, or remote script you add runs with your application's or build's privileges, so its identity, provenance, and install-time behavior are part of your attack surface.
learningObjectives: Evaluate a newly added dependency for provenance, maintenance, and whether it is the package actually intended
Explain how lockfiles and pinned versions make installs reproducible and limit surprise upgrades
Identify install-time scripts and transitive dependencies as code that runs with developer or CI access
recognitionSignals: new dependencies added to package.json, requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, go.mod, or similar manifests
loose version ranges or 'latest' for newly added dependencies
postinstall or other package lifecycle scripts
remote scripts piped to a shell or unpinned third-party actions in build steps
misconceptionPatterns: Assuming a package is legitimate because an AI assistant suggested it or its name looks plausible
Believing installing a package only downloads code and never executes it
Believing a popular, trusted package cannot ship a compromised release

concepts.title: Prompt injection and untrusted model output
concepts.summary: Any text an LLM reads — user messages, documents, web pages, tool results — can carry instructions the model may follow, and model output is itself untrusted input; because no delimiter reliably prevents this, safety comes from limiting what the model can do and validating what it produces.
learningObjectives: Identify untrusted text that reaches a model's context in a change, including retrieved documents, tool results, and repository content
Explain why delimiters and system-prompt instructions reduce but do not prevent injected instructions from being followed
Identify model output flowing into privileged sinks such as SQL, HTML or markdown rendering, shell commands, tool calls, or outbound requests
Design mitigations that bound impact: minimal tool permissions, schema-validated structured output, and human confirmation for consequential actions
recognitionSignals: user-supplied or retrieved content concatenated or templated into LLM prompts
LLM tool or function-calling handlers that write data, send messages, or fetch URLs
model output parsed and passed to database queries, rendered as HTML or markdown, executed, or used as URLs
structured-output schemas or validation applied to model responses
misconceptionPatterns: Believing delimiters or 'ignore instructions in the following text' prompts reliably stop prompt injection
Treating model output as trusted because the application wrote the prompt
Believing injected instructions can only come from the direct user rather than from documents, web pages, or tool results the model reads
Granting an agent broad tool permissions on the assumption that the model will refuse malicious instructions
